narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 worked in the opposite direction and was the second most important factor. This is well above the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model saw it as a meaningful reason you might still succeed. Your LSAT score of 37 was the third strongest influence. It sits almost exactly at the average for accepted applicants and therefore pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, but not enough to overcome the effect of your third-year ranking.

Taken together, the model concluded that your overall profile pointed more toward bar exam difficulty than success. To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your study habits and class performance in the remaining part of law school so that your final ranking rises. You may also want to consider full-time study rather than part-time work, as nearly 93% of accepted students pursued full-time enrollment. Retaking the LSAT or targeted bar-prep courses could further demonstrate readiness on a future application.
